stories.headline: Kenyan Doomsday Cult Leader Paul Mackenzie Sentenced to 200 Years for Murdering 191 People
stories.summary:
A Kenyan court sentenced cult leader Paul Mackenzie to 200 years in prison for the murders of 191 people, all but one of them children. Mackenzie was convicted alongside 28 others of instructing followers to starve their children to death so they could "meet Jesus." Justice Diana Mochache said he bore the "primary criminal culpability" for ordering the fasts, in one of the world's deadliest episodes of cult activity.

The court imposed 100 years for homicide and another 100 years for offences related to starvation. Sentences within each category run concurrently, but the two sets run consecutively. Prosecutors had sought the death penalty, and the judge ruled the case met the threshold for its consideration. She declined to impose it, saying capital punishment would eliminate any prospect of rehabilitation. Kenya has not carried out an execution since 1987.

The 28 co-accused, including guards who enforced the fasting orders and gravediggers who helped conceal bodies, received sentences of up to 160 years. Justice Mochache called the killings "cold and calculated" and said the perpetrators showed no remorse. Followers had believed Mackenzie was "Jesus's mouthpiece," and those who opposed his teachings were beaten to death.

Mackenzie was arrested in 2023 after more than 400 bodies were found in shallow graves in Shakahola forest near the Kenyan coast. He was convicted on 19 October and had pleaded not guilty, insisting nobody was forced to die. He still faces separate manslaughter and terrorism charges, which he denies.

stories.headline: Two Dead, Including a Child, After Bus Crash in Eastern France
stories.summary:
A bus crash in eastern France on Friday killed a child and a young adult and left three people in critical condition. The bus was traveling between Lyon and Bourg-en-Bresse when it crashed around 7:00 a.m. local time in the town of Lent, about 55 kilometers from the Swiss border. Mayor Yves Cristin said the bus left the road and hit a tree in a ditch.

The bus carried 43 passengers, including 15 children. Authorities identified the dead as a young girl, whose reported age varied, and an 18-year-old man. Thirteen others suffered minor injuries. More than 100 firefighters and 50 gendarmes responded, and medical helicopters took the seriously injured to a specialized hospital.

The Bourg-en-Bresse prosecutor opened an investigation on charges of road homicide and aggravated road traffic injuries. The driver was hospitalized and has not yet been questioned. Transport Minister Philippe Tabarot said initial tests found no alcohol or drugs. The mayor said there was some fog and the road was wet, but no major difficulties. Tabarot noted the bus did not operate exclusively on school routes, though many schoolchildren were aboard.

stories.headline: Musk Signals Tesla Will Wind Down Cybertruck Production in Texas
stories.summary:
Elon Musk said Tesla will wind down Cybertruck production at its Texas factory next year to make room for its self-driving Cybercab. He did not say whether Tesla will stop making the vehicle entirely or move production elsewhere. Lead engineer Wes Morrill appeared to suggest it was being discontinued, writing that the Cybertruck "lives on through Cybercab."

Responding to a fan lamenting that the truck would be discontinued, Musk replied "true," adding that the Cybertruck fleet will be around for a long time. The vehicle has long been a passion project for Musk, who called it the best product Tesla has made as recently as April.

The Cybertruck launched in 2023 after delays, and sales have been disappointing despite Musk's claim of 146,000 orders in 2019. Several recalls, including one in 2025 affecting more than 46,000 vehicles, added to its troubles. Prices rose from a promised level to $61,000 for a fully equipped model, and the 2026 Cyberbeast costs $102,000.

stories.headline: Update: Indonesia's Presidential Wiretapping Scandal Widens as Chief of Staff Is Sacked and Treason Probed
stories.summary:
Indonesian authorities are investigating possible treason after announcing that President Prabowo Subianto's phone conversations may have been spied on. Chief of staff Listyo Sigit Prabowo, who is not related to the president, was arrested Tuesday with two senior police officers and was sacked from his post, to which he had been appointed last month. On Thursday evening police named a fourth suspect, Slamet Uliandi of the national police criminal investigation unit, who was not detained because of ill health after a stroke.

The suspects allegedly entered phone numbers, including the president's, into the police electronic surveillance system without a warrant or case report. Authorities believe the operation dates to 2025, when Listyo was national police chief, and say it also targeted politicians, journalists, NGO representatives and businesspeople. A presidential spokesperson said it could amount to treason, which carries life imprisonment or death, though Indonesia has not executed anyone in a decade.

The motive remains unclear. Some analysts see a widening rift between Prabowo and predecessor Joko Widodo, to whom Listyo is considered close. Police chief Suyudi Ario Seto said the probe is purely law enforcement and unrelated to rivalries.

stories.headline: Somalia's Supreme Court Rules President's Term Extension Unlawful, Voids Chief Justice's Dismissal
stories.summary:
Somalia's Supreme Court ruled on Thursday that President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud unlawfully extended his term, deepening a confrontation between the presidency and the judiciary. The ruling came a day after Mohamud dismissed Chief Justice Bashe Yusuf Ahmed, a move the court declared "null and void" on the grounds that the president lacked the authority to take it. The president has appointed Ibrahim Idle Suleiman, who previously held the post, as a replacement.

Mohamud's four-year mandate expired in May, but his administration extended it by a year through legal changes approved by parliament in March. The court held that the constitutional changes cannot be applied retrospectively to his current term. It ordered political leaders to agree on an electoral plan within 30 days and to hold elections within 90 days, which could upend government plans for nationwide polls next year. The electoral commission has scheduled parliamentary elections for 15 April 2027 and a presidential vote a month later, a timetable rejected by opposition groups and the regional administrations of Puntland and Jubaland.

The presidency said the dismissal followed complaints about the administration of justice and was meant to achieve a transparent judiciary. Mohamud argues his reforms are needed to move Somalia toward direct elections, replacing the clan-based system in which elders pick representatives. Opposition groups accuse him of using the changes to prolong his rule. Former President Sharif Sheikh Ahmed welcomed the ruling and urged a consensus approach, while former Prime Minister Hassan Ali Khaire accused the president of sending security forces to the court and trying to arrest the chief justice. AFP could not verify that claim, though photographs in Somali media appeared to show armed personnel inside the compound.

The crisis comes in a country that has not held nationwide direct elections since 1969 and where al-Shabaab still controls many rural areas.

stories.headline: Three States Carry Out Executions in One Day as Florida Ties Annual Record
stories.summary:
Florida, Indiana and Alabama each carried out an execution on the same day, a rare occurrence last seen before this year in 2010. Florida executed Jesse Guardado, 64, by three-drug injection at a state prison in Starke, with death pronounced at 6:13 p.m. It was the state's 19th execution of the year, tying its record. Guardado had pleaded guilty to fatally stabbing 75-year-old Jackie Malone in her Walton County home in 2004.

Hours earlier, Indiana executed a man for killing two children in a 2010 house fire, and Alabama carried out the last lethal injection of the day for the killing of an elderly man and woman during a home robbery in 1991. It was the second time since August that three states executed prisoners on a single day. The U.S. has carried out 35 executions this year, more than half of them in Florida, and capital punishment has faced renewed scrutiny after Tennessee's failed execution of Christa Pike in September.

The executions came as California Gov. Gavin Newsom announced he will commute all 548 death sentences in his state, saying "state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California's values." Outgoing Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis, a Republican, has signed the warrants for the state's record pace and says he wants to bring justice to victims' families who have often waited decades. Florida will set a new record if two more executions planned later this year proceed. Patrick Malone, the victim's son, questioned opponents of the death penalty, asking whether they consider the aftermath victims' families endure.

stories.headline: Update: Satellite Images Show Iran Rebuilding and Digging Near Missile Bases
stories.summary:
Iran appears to be undertaking significant new construction near at least two major missile sites and repairing bases damaged in months of US and Israeli air strikes, according to analysis of November satellite imagery. Analysts at the British intelligence firm MAIAR, speaking to BBC Verify, pointed to digging and new buildings at the Garmdareh base in Karaj near Tehran and the Shahroud base in the north. At least 12 other military sites show signs of repair.

At Kermanshah, new roofs have been built on destroyed buildings, and debris has been cleared at the Parchin complex, which has been repeatedly repaired despite successive strikes. Analysts said work at Parchin's Taleghan 2 facility includes a repaired underground bunker reinforced with concrete. Researchers at the Foreign Policy Research Institute said Karaj appears to show a new portal for an underground facility. Former CIA analyst Jim Lamson said the Shahroud excavations could relate to missile production, with the Revolutionary Guards probably seeking to move production underground.

The findings come as speculation grows that the US could resume attacks on Iran after this week's midterm elections. Vice President JD Vance said Wednesday that the war's unpopularity cost Republicans in the vote and may have cost the party Senate control for six years. Earlier this week US officials described strikes on Qeshm Island as limited and defensive, and President Trump has acknowledged the war's role in the Republican defeat while defending his decision to launch it. Iranian parliament speaker Mohammed Bagher Ghalibaf has publicly endorsed a message tied to the conflict, and the administration is weighing a deal or renewed strikes.

stories.headline: Nigerian Court Invalidates Opposition Candidate Atiku Abubakar's Nomination
stories.summary:
Nigeria's Federal High Court in Abuja has removed the leadership of the opposition African Democratic Congress and ruled that the nomination of its presidential candidate, former Vice President Atiku Abubakar, is invalid. Justice Peter Lifu issued the judgment Thursday in a case brought by former ADC deputy chairman Nafiu Bala Gombe, who argued that interim chairman David Mark and others had not been elected at a national convention. Gombe said he should have taken over after the previous chairman resigned in 2025.

The ADC called the ruling a calculated attempt to cripple the opposition and said it will appeal. Abubakar, 79, said the decision showed the "panic was real" among those threatened by his candidacy, noting it came a day after a large crowd welcomed him at his campaign launch in Sokoto. He questioned why a new case reopened a dispute a different judge settled in July, when Justice Musa Liman found Mark was chosen lawfully.

Presidential elections are scheduled for 16 January, with President Bola Tinubu facing challengers including Abubakar and former Anambra governor Peter Obi. The electoral commission has issued its final candidate list, which includes Abubakar with former Rivers State governor Rotimi Amaechi as running mate. The ADC is seen as the strongest opposition vehicle, having drawn many influential politicians opposed to Tinubu's ruling All Progressives Congress. The legal fight could create uncertainty for the ticket and for ADC candidates in other races as the appeal proceeds.
